lead: This unit is about the direction of processes: why heat flows from hot to cold, why work can become heat but not fully back, and how entropy measures that one-way loss. After it you can test engine and refrigerator claims against the second law, compute entropy changes and lost work, and analyse steam power and refrigeration cycles.
about: This unit gives thermodynamics its direction. It starts with the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the second law, uses them to rate heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps, and finds the best possible performance in the Carnot cycle, which also defines the thermodynamic temperature scale. Entropy and the Clausius inequality turn the statements into a property you can calculate; the control-volume entropy balance applies it to turbines, compressors and heat exchangers; the third law fixes its zero; lost work prices every irreversibility; and the microscopic view explains what entropy counts. Steam power plants and refrigeration and liquefaction cycles are the two big applications, worked with real steam and refrigerant data.

chapters.idea: The second law says no device can convert a single heat reservoir completely into work, and no refrigerator can move heat from cold to hot without work input.
chapters.depth: State the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius forms, define heat reservoir, cyclic device, thermal efficiency η = W/Q_H, and COP. Show their equivalence by contradiction using simple energy balances. Some syllabi call these the Kelvin–Planck statement and the Clausius statement; also mention perpetual motion machine of the second kind.

figure.title: Second-law statements
figure.aria: A real engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, rejects some heat to a cold reservoir and delivers work; a dashed perfect engine tries to deliver all the heat as work.

chapters.example: A cyclic engine takes 100 kJ from a 600 K reservoir and rejects 60 kJ to a 300 K reservoir. Find W, η, and check whether it violates the Kelvin–Planck statement. Answer: W = 40 kJ, η = 40%, and it is allowed because Q_C = 60 kJ is greater than zero.
chapters.trap: Thinking an engine with η = 100% is only inefficient; the second law forbids it, not the first law.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: first law energy balance, cyclic process, heat and work.
chapters.leave: Carnot efficiency and entropy proof to 3.3–3.4; engine hardware to 3.8.

chapters.idea: A heat engine makes work from heat flow, while a refrigerator or heat pump uses work to move heat from cold to hot; all three obey the same energy balance.
chapters.depth: Draw Q_H, Q_C and W with consistent signs. Define η, COP_R and COP_HP; show COP_HP = COP_R + 1. Discuss room air conditioners and domestic refrigerators as examples. Some syllabi call a heat pump a reversed heat engine.

figure.title: Heat pump and refrigerator
figure.aria: A refrigerator or heat pump uses work input to move heat from a cold space to a warm space, with Q_H equal to Q_C plus W.

chapters.example: A refrigerator removes 5 kW from a cold space at 4 °C and rejects heat to a kitchen at 32 °C. Its compressor draws 2 kW. Find Q_H and COP_R. Answer: Q_H = 7 kW and COP_R = 5/2 = 2.5.
chapters.trap: Mixing Q_H and Q_C, or using COP = W/Q_C instead of Q_C/W.
chapters.leave: Carnot COP to 3.3; actual cycle analysis to 3.9.

chapters.idea: The Carnot cycle is a reversible cycle between two reservoirs, and no real cycle between the same reservoirs can be more efficient.
chapters.depth: Describe the four Carnot steps using an ideal gas: two isothermal and two adiabatic. State the Carnot theorems and define the thermodynamic temperature scale by Q_H/Q_C = T_H/T_C for a reversible engine. Derive η_C = 1 − T_C/T_H and the reversed Carnot COP. Some syllabi call this the Carnot principle.

figure.aria: A straight line falls from efficiency 1 at T_C/T_H equal 0 to efficiency 0 at T_C/T_H equal 1.

chapters.example: A Carnot engine operates between 600 K and 300 K and takes 1000 kJ from the hot reservoir. Find η, W and Q_C. Answer: η = 1 − 300/600 = 50%, W = 500 kJ, Q_C = 500 kJ.
chapters.trap: Using Celsius temperatures in η = 1 − T_C/T_H; temperatures must be in kelvin.
chapters.prereq: 3.1–3.2; Unit 2 ideal-gas isothermal and adiabatic processes; Unit 1 reversible process.
chapters.leave: Entropy proof to 3.4; real Rankine efficiency to 3.8.

chapters.idea: Entropy is a state property whose change for a reversible path is ∫δQ_rev/T, and the Clausius inequality makes the total entropy change of an isolated system never decrease.
chapters.depth: Define S and dS = δQ_rev/T. Calculate ΔS for an ideal gas in T,V and T,P forms, for phase change as ΔH/T, and for heating as ∫C_p dT/T. State the Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0: zero for reversible, negative for irreversible. Some syllabi call this the mathematical statement of the second law.

figure.title: Clausius inequality
figure.aria: A cyclic device feeds the Clausius integral; zero means reversible, negative means irreversible, and positive is impossible.

chapters.example: One mole of ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally from 10 L to 20 L. Find ΔS. Answer: ΔS = R ln(V2/V1) = 8.314 × ln 2 = 5.76 J/K.
chapters.trap: Using irreversible Q/T in dS; entropy change uses a reversible path between the same states, not the actual irreversible heat.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 Carnot cycle; Unit 1 first law; Unit 2 ideal gas.
chapters.leave: Open-system entropy balance to 3.5; lost work to 3.7; detailed tables to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: For an open control volume, entropy in by flow and heat plus entropy generated must equal entropy out plus accumulation.
chapters.depth: Write dS_CV/dt = Σ m_i s_i − Σ m_e s_e + Σ Q_j/T_j + S_gen. For steady state set accumulation to zero. Define specific entropy s and entropy generation rate S_gen ≥ 0. Apply to adiabatic turbines, compressors, nozzles and heat exchangers. Some syllabi call this the second law for a control volume.

figure.title: Entropy balance on a control volume
figure.aria: Entropy enters a steady control volume with the inlet stream and heat transfer, leaves with the outlet stream, and is generated inside by irreversibility.

chapters.example: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at 2 MPa, 400 °C with s = 7.0 kJ/kg·K and leaves at 0.1 MPa with s = 7.4 kJ/kg·K. The mass flow is 2 kg/s. Find S_gen. Answer: steady adiabatic gives S_gen = m(s_out − s_in) = 2(7.4 − 7.0) = 0.8 kW/K.
chapters.trap: Forgetting S_gen and treating an adiabatic real turbine as isentropic.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 entropy; Unit 1 steady-flow mass and energy balances.
chapters.leave: Exergy and lost work to 3.7; detailed turbine design to 3.8.

chapters.idea: The third law fixes entropy zero at absolute zero for a perfect crystal, so all absolute entropies can be measured from that reference.
chapters.depth: State the Nernst heat theorem and the third law: S → 0 as T → 0 for a perfect ordered crystal. Compute absolute entropy by integrating C_p/T from 0 K. Mention residual entropy in disordered crystals such as CO and glasses. State that absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.

figure.aria: Entropy rises from zero at 0 K following a cubic low-temperature curve and reaches about 0.33 J/mol K at 10 K.

chapters.example: A crystal obeys C_p = aT³ at low temperature with a = 0.001 J mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴. Using S(0) = 0, find S at 10 K. Answer: S = ∫0^10 (C_p/T)dT = ∫0^10 aT² dT = aT³/3 = 0.001 × 1000/3 = 0.33 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
chapters.trap: Using S = 0 at 0 °C or 298 K; the third-law zero is 0 K.
chapters.leave: Statistical counting to 3.10; reaction absolute entropies to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: Every real process destroys some work, equal to T₀ S_gen, so ideal work is the reversible work and lost work is the gap.
chapters.depth: Advanced: only a few universities teach this as exergy or availability. Define dead-state temperature T₀ and ideal work W_ideal = ΔH − T₀ΔS for steady flow. State the Gouy–Stodola theorem W_lost = T₀ S_gen. Connect lost work to exergy destruction. Keep the treatment short and avoid full exergy balances.

figure.aria: Lost work rises linearly with entropy generation; at S_gen equal 0.222 kJ/K it is about 66.7 kJ when T₀ is 300 K.

chapters.example: Heat of 1000 kJ passes from a reservoir at 500 K to a reservoir at 450 K. The surroundings are at 300 K. Find S_gen and lost work. Answer: S_gen = 1000(1/450 − 1/500) = 0.222 kJ/K; W_lost = 300 × 0.222 = 66.7 kJ.
chapters.trap: Adding lost work to actual work instead of subtracting it; lost work is the work you could have had.
chapters.leave: Full exergy analysis and economics to a later design course; cycle hardware to 3.8–3.9.

chapters.idea: A steam power plant converts heat into work in a Rankine cycle; its efficiency is set by boiler and condenser conditions and improved by reheat and regeneration.
chapters.depth: Describe the Rankine cycle: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser. Draw T–s and h–s sketches. Use η = (W_t − W_p)/Q_in and steam tables. Compare ideal and actual turbine and pump. Explain reheat, regenerative feed heating and condenser-pressure effects. Some syllabi call this the steam power plant cycle.

figure.title: Rankine cycle
figure.aria: Water is heated in the boiler, expands through the turbine to make work, condenses in the condenser and is pumped back to the boiler.

chapters.example: In an ideal Rankine cycle, steam enters the turbine with h = 3200 kJ/kg and leaves with h = 2100 kJ/kg. Condensate leaves the condenser with h = 200 kJ/kg, and pump work is 20 kJ/kg. Find net work, heat added, cycle efficiency and heat rejected. Answer: W_net = 1100 − 20 = 1080 kJ/kg; Q_in = 3200 − 220 = 2980 kJ/kg; η = 1080/2980 = 36.2%; Q_out = 1900 kJ/kg.
chapters.trap: Using turbine work alone as net work; subtract pump work, and take Q_in from feedwater enthalpy after the pump.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 Carnot cycle; Unit 2 PVT; Unit 4 steam tables and property diagrams; Unit 1 steady-flow energy.
chapters.leave: Refrigeration to 3.9; detailed boiler and turbine design to later courses.

chapters.idea: Refrigeration and liquefaction use work to move heat from a cold region to a warm one; the vapour-compression cycle is the common practical cycle.
chapters.depth: Describe the vapour-compression cycle: compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator. Define COP_R and COP_HP; compare with Carnot COP. Mention actual versus ideal cycles and Joule–Thomson expansion. Introduce Linde and Claude liquefaction cycles only at a block level.

figure.title: Vapour-compression cycle
figure.aria: Refrigerant evaporates while taking heat from the cold space, is compressed, condenses while rejecting heat, and passes through an expansion valve back to the evaporator.

chapters.example: A refrigerator removes 5 kW from a cold space at 250 K and rejects heat to surroundings at 300 K. Its actual COP is 2.5. Find compressor work, Carnot COP and minimum work. Answer: W = 5/2.5 = 2 kW; COP_Carnot = 250/(300 − 250) = 5; W_min = 5/5 = 1 kW.
chapters.trap: Using Celsius temperatures in the Carnot COP, or forgetting COP_HP = COP_R + 1.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 devices; 3.3 Carnot COP; Unit 4 property tables.
chapters.leave: Detailed liquefaction cycles and cryogenic design to later courses; exergy to 3.7.

chapters.idea: Entropy is a count of microscopic arrangements: S = k_B ln Ω, so a macrostate with more microstates has higher entropy.
chapters.depth: Define microstate and macrostate. State the Boltzmann relation S = k_B ln Ω and explain Ω as the number of accessible microstates at fixed energy, volume and particles. Connect this to the third law: one microstate at 0 K gives S = 0. Mention residual entropy in disordered solids. Some syllabi call this the statistical interpretation of entropy.

figure.aria: Entropy rises as the logarithm of the number of microstates, from zero at one microstate to about 4.6 when Ω is 100.

chapters.example: Two distinguishable particles can each sit in one of two boxes, giving four equally likely microstates. Find the entropy. Answer: Ω = 4, S = k_B ln 4 = 1.386 k_B = 1.386 × 1.381 × 10⁻²³ = 1.91 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
chapters.trap: Thinking entropy is only disorder; it is the number of accessible microstates at fixed energy, volume and particles.
chapters.leave: Statistical-mechanics derivations and quantum gases to a later course.
